claims.text: The overall stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is governed by temperature-dependent internal residual stresses generated by mismatches among the intrinsic thermal expansion coefficients of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch residual stresses promote local lattice distortions.
The resulting lattice distortions alter dislocation mobility and elastic modulus over different temperature regimes.
A high-temperature anneal above 1000 °C will minimize thermal-expansion-mismatch-induced residual stresses relative to the as-solidified condition.
The magnitude of local lattice distortion and internal residual stress varies with temperature and processing history.
Internal residual-stress fields modify resistance to dislocation glide.
At high temperature, residual-stress-induced lattice heterogeneity creates localized regions with lower activation energy for creep.
At lower temperatures, residual-stress-induced distortions act as dislocation obstacles and enhance hardness after cold work.
Residual-stress-induced distortions alter the effective elastic modulus of HfNbTaTiZr.
Aging at 600–800 °C may activate atomic rearrangement, such as local short-range ordering, that amplifies the residual-stress effects.
Stress-relieved samples will have a more homogeneous lattice and reduced barriers to dislocation movement.
Annealed samples will exhibit lower creep rates at 1250 °C than the as-solidified baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit lower microhardness after identical cold rolling than the as-solidified baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit a more linear or less anomalous elastic-modulus dependence between 293 and 1100 K.
Annealed samples will exhibit diminished hardening after aging at 600–800 °C.
The predicted differences between annealed and as-solidified samples will be most pronounced in the high-temperature creep and intermediate-temperature aging regimes.
Previously reported HfNbTaTiZr behavior includes increased hardness after cold rolling, nonlinear elastic-modulus variation from 293 to 1100 K, and aging-induced hardening at 600–800 °C.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch residual stresses dominate the behavior only in the absence of significant secondary-phase formation or oxidation.
